# What Is Shadow AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-shadow-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-05 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Shadow AI is the use of AI tools at work without the organisation's approval or oversight. Surveys suggest it is the norm rather than the exception, and IBM-sponsored research links it to costlier breaches. Bans rarely work; an approved alternative, a short policy and an inventory do.

Shadow AI is the use of AI tools at work without the organisation's knowledge, approval or oversight: a personal chatbot account used for client emails, a free notetaker joining sales calls, a browser extension reading the CRM. It is usually well-meant. The risk is that company and client data flows to services nobody has assessed, and that decisions get made with tools nobody can audit.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What shadow AI means

The term follows "shadow IT", the long-standing problem of staff adopting software without IT's involvement. Shadow AI is the same pattern applied to AI: tools adopted by individuals or teams, outside procurement and security review.

It differs from shadow IT in one respect that matters. Most AI tools work by receiving content. Using one means sending it text, files, call audio or screen contents. A spreadsheet app used without approval stores data; an AI assistant used without approval processes it, and the provider's terms decide what happens next.

| Form of shadow AI | Typical commercial example | Main exposure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Personal chatbot accounts | Pasting a client's RFP into a free assistant | Client confidential data leaves the firm |
| Meeting notetakers | A bot joins a prospect call from a rep's own account | Recording without consent; transcripts stored externally |
| Browser extensions | An AI writing aid with access to every page, including the CRM | Broad read access to systems |
| AI features in approved tools | A new AI option switched on in an existing app | Terms change without review |
| Unregistered agents | A rep connects an agent to their inbox | Actions taken in the firm's name, unlogged |

## Why it happens and what it costs

### It is the norm

Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index, a survey of 31,000 people in 31 countries, found 75% of knowledge workers used AI at work and 78% of AI users brought their own tools. The same report found 60% of leaders worried their company lacked a plan and vision for AI. When the firm has no approved option, staff find their own.

Gartner's survey of 302 cybersecurity leaders, run between March and May 2025, found 69% suspected or had evidence of employees using prohibited public generative AI. Gartner predicts that by 2030 more than 40% of enterprises will experience security or compliance incidents linked to unauthorised shadow AI.

### Breaches cost more

IBM's Cost of a Data Breach 2025, researched by the Ponemon Institute across 600 breached organisations, found one in five reported a breach due to shadow AI. Organisations with high levels of shadow AI saw breach costs an average of $670,000 higher than those with low or none. Among breached organisations, 63% had no AI governance policy or were still writing one.

### Commercial teams are exposed

Sales and account teams handle exactly the data that should not leave: client lists, pricing, proposals, call recordings. They are also under time pressure and quick to adopt tools that save it. A drafting assistant on a personal account is the commonest form of shadow AI in commercial work.

> Shadow AI is a signal that people need a tool. The fix is a better approved option, not a louder ban.

## How to bring it into the open

Gartner's recommendations are to set enterprise-wide policies for AI tool use, audit regularly for shadow AI activity, and add generative AI risk to SaaS assessments. NIST's generative AI profile adds the inventory: enumerate the organisation's AI systems (action GV-1.6-001). For a mid-size firm, that becomes five steps.

| Step | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Ask, without penalty | Survey staff on which AI tools they use and for what; amnesty gets honest answers |
| Provide the approved option | Choose an enterprise assistant with data protections and make it easy to get |
| Publish a one-page policy | Approved tools, data that must never be entered, what needs review |
| Keep an inventory | Every AI tool and agent, its owner, its data access and its terms |
| Check quarterly | Review expense claims, browser extensions, OAuth grants and meeting bots |

The sequence matters. A policy without an approved tool drives use further underground. An approved tool without a policy leaves people guessing what they can paste into it. Gateway 0 in The Build Order, which settles the owner, the suite and the CRM before any AI tool is bought, exists partly for this reason.

## lowob takeaways

- **Assume it exists.** Surveys show most AI users bring their own tools.
- **It costs real money.** IBM's 2025 study puts the added breach cost of high shadow AI use at $670,000 on average.
- **Offer before you forbid.** An approved assistant reduces shadow use more than a ban.
- **Inventory everything.** Tools, agents, owners, data access and terms, reviewed quarterly.
